assertion.prompt: Why does the measured origin licensing deficit in patient cells fail to predict S-phase progression rate or clinical severity?
attaches_to: pathophysiology#Delayed S-Phase Entry and Reduced Cell Proliferation
assertion.rationale: Licensing capacity is impaired in all MGORS patient cells regardless of gene, yet it does not correlate with the rate of S-phase progression, and the clinical severity gradient (ORC1 and ORC4 most severe) is not explained by licensing measurements alone. This uncoupling is a central unresolved question of MGORS pathogenesis and is what motivates the parallel non-replicative arms, notably the centriole and ciliogenesis route. Whether the non-canonical roles of these proteins, tissue-specific proliferative demand, or something else supplies the missing explanatory variable is unknown. One partial answer already exists for the ORC1 arm specifically: the BAH domain reads H4K20me2 to target ORC to origins, so BAH mutations remove a chromatin-targeting step rather than simply lowering licensing capacity. Whether an analogous upstream-targeting defect distinguishes the other severe arms has not been tested.

proposed_experiments.name: Parallel licensing, fork, cell-cycle and ciliogenesis phenotyping across an isogenic MGORS allelic series
proposed_experiments.description: Measure licensed origin density, fork speed, cell cycle length and ciliogenesis competence in parallel across an isogenic allelic series spanning the licensing module (ORC1, ORC4, CDT1) and the CMG module (CDC45, GINS2, GINS3), in a developmentally relevant proliferating cell type such as iPSC-derived chondroprogenitors, and test which measure predicts differentiation output.
proposed_experiments.decision_criterion: The measure whose variation across the allelic series best predicts chondrogenic differentiation output identifies the rate-limiting step.
supporting_outcome: Ciliogenesis competence predicts differentiation output better than licensed origin density, supporting the non-replicative arm as the severity determinant
refuting_outcome: Licensed origin density predicts differentiation output linearly, restoring the simple licensing-deficit model

selected_evidence.snippet: Thus, the replicative capacity in MGS patient cells does not correlate with clinical manifestation.

assertion.prompt: Why do roughly a third of endocrinologically assessed individuals with MGORS show a decreased response to growth hormone stimulation testing, when the growth failure of the syndrome is largely growth-hormone independent?
attaches_to: phenotypes#Decreased response to growth hormone stimulation test
assertion.rationale: Growth hormone therapy is ineffective in most individuals and growth velocity normalizes spontaneously after the first year of life, which points to a cell-intrinsic, GH-independent growth deficit. Yet 35.3% of endocrinologically assessed cases in a review selected for endocrinopathy or hormonal therapy had reported growth hormone deficiency, and 42.9% had low IGF-1. The abstract does not give feature-specific denominators. No study has established how a replication-initiation defect would produce a pituitary secretory abnormality - candidate routes include reduced somatotroph progenitor expansion during pituitary development and ascertainment bias in an endocrine-referred case literature - so this phenotype is deliberately left without a causal edge from the growth-restriction node rather than wired through an unsupported intermediate.

proposed_experiments.name: Systematic pituitary imaging and GH-axis phenotyping in molecularly confirmed MGORS
proposed_experiments.description: In a molecularly confirmed MGORS cohort unselected for endocrine referral, combine pituitary MRI volumetry with standardized GH stimulation testing, IGF-1 measurement and overnight spontaneous GH secretion profiling, stratified by gene arm.
proposed_experiments.decision_criterion: Reduced pituitary volume co-segregating with abnormal stimulation responses would support a developmental somatotroph deficit; normal imaging and secretion in an unselected cohort would attribute the reported GHD rate to ascertainment bias.
supporting_outcome: Pituitary hypoplasia and blunted stimulated GH secretion cluster in the same individuals and gene arms
refuting_outcome: Unselected cohort shows normal GH-axis measures, reclassifying the reported GHD rate as referral bias

selected_evidence.snippet: Growth hormone treatment is ineffective in most patients with MGS, but may be effective in patients in whom growth continues to decrease after the first year of life (usually growth velocity normalizes after the first year) and with low levels of IGF1.

assertion.prompt: How do MGORS replication defects alter alveolar development?
assertion.rationale: The clinical and genotype-phenotype evidence establishes emphysema, but neither disproportionate tissue growth nor cartilage chondroinduction identifies an alveolar mechanism. Co-occurrence with airway malacia does not establish a causal route to either finding.

selected_evidence.snippet:
Respiratory tract anomalies are relatively frequent. Con-
genital pulmonary emphysema was reported in 43 % (12/
28) of patients with MGS.

assertion.prompt: What determines the tissue selectivity of MGORS, so that external ear cartilage, the patella, mammary tissue and the external genitalia are affected out of proportion to overall stature?
attaches_to: pathophysiology#Reduced Hedgehog Signaling and Impaired Chondroinduction
assertion.rationale: A uniform, cell-autonomous replication deficit should scale all tissues together, yet the phenotype is strikingly selective, and it is that selectivity, not the short stature, that makes MGORS clinically recognizable. Candidate explanations include narrow developmental windows of unusually intense proliferation in these structures and the ciliary Hedgehog and chondroinduction arm, but no cell-type-resolved human data exist.

proposed_experiments.name: Cell-type-resolved mapping of proliferative demand in MGORS-vulnerable human embryonic structures
proposed_experiments.description: Build a cell-type-resolved map of proliferative demand and replication stress in human embryonic auricular cartilage, patellar anlage and mammary bud, and test whether a licensing-deficient background preferentially depletes progenitors in exactly those compartments.
proposed_experiments.decision_criterion: Preferential progenitor depletion in the MGORS-vulnerable compartments relative to matched control compartments supports proliferative demand as the selectivity mechanism.
supporting_outcome: MGORS-vulnerable compartments show the highest proliferative demand and the greatest progenitor loss under a licensing-deficient background
refuting_outcome: Progenitor loss is uniform across compartments, implicating a tissue-specific signaling requirement instead

selected_evidence.snippet: we highlight that growth is disproportionately affected in certain structures

assertion.prompt: Does the GINS3 D24 mouse model, which is embryonic lethal, faithfully represent human GINS3-related Meier-Gorlin syndrome, in which affected individuals survive?
attaches_to: pathophysiology#Global Prenatal and Postnatal Growth Restriction
assertion.rationale: Homozygous D24 mouse embryos show intrauterine growth retardation and do not survive to birth, while the seven humans reported with the corresponding hypomorphic GINS3 genotypes survive with an MGORS-like phenotype. The mouse therefore recapitulates growth restriction but overshoots on severity, so mechanistic inferences drawn from it, particularly the accelerated senescence of the derived fibroblasts, may reflect a more complete loss of function than human disease alleles produce.

proposed_experiments.name: Humanized GINS3 allelic series calibrating mouse severity against patient fibroblasts
proposed_experiments.description: Generate a mouse allelic series carrying the specific human GINS3 hypomorphic substitutions at matched residues, and compare residual protein level, fork progression and senescence markers against patient-derived fibroblasts to calibrate where the human alleles sit on the murine severity curve.
proposed_experiments.decision_criterion: Concordance of residual protein level, fork speed and senescence markers between the humanized mice and patient fibroblasts establishes the translational validity of the murine readouts.
supporting_outcome: Humanized alleles produce viable mice whose fibroblast phenotypes match patient cells, validating the model
refuting_outcome: Humanized alleles remain lethal or produce senescence far exceeding patient cells, confining the model to loss-of-function extremes

selected_evidence.snippet: We further showed that mouse embryos homozygous for a D24 variant presented intrauterine growth retardation and did not survive to birth

assertion.prompt: What causes recurrent childhood respiratory infections in MGORS?
assertion.rationale: The clinical review documents childhood recurrence and later resolution, but does not distinguish structural airway, aspiration or immune causes. The GINS3-associated neutropenia finding must not be generalized to the pre-replication-complex patients underlying the 2015 review.

selected_evidence.snippet:
Recurrent respiratory tract infections occur often during
childhood, but disappear thereafter.

assertion.prompt: What explains clitoromegaly with hypoplastic labia in MGORS?
assertion.rationale: Clitoromegaly with hypoplastic labia is reported in the endocrine-selected case literature despite normal reported gonadal hormones. A small-growth pattern in neighboring genital structures does not establish a mechanism for clitoral enlargement, so no growth-failure edge is asserted.

selected_evidence.snippet: Among females, all post-pubertal cases had mammary hypoplasia, while 23.5% had clitoromegaly with hypoplastic labia.

assertion.prompt: How do replication-initiation defects produce malacia at different airway levels in MGORS?
assertion.rationale: The clinical review documents the three airway sites as a combined 10/24 frequency but does not identify the airway cell type or developmental process responsible. The existing chondroinduction experiments address ciliary signaling in cell models; they do not establish an airway-specific route in patients. These findings remain without causal in-edges.

selected_evidence.snippet:
Bronchomalacia, laryngomalacia and/or tra-
cheomalacia are reported in 42 % (10/24) of subjects.

assertion.prompt: What accounts for contractures, knee hyperextension, hypermobility and flat feet in MGORS?
assertion.rationale: Contractures including club feet are documented in 7/30 assessed cases. The clinical review does not establish that they are caused by the patellar-growth defect or the cell-model chondroinduction abnormality. Joint developmental mechanisms remain unassigned rather than inferred from co-occurrence with other skeletal findings. Genu recurvatum, joint hypermobility and pes planus are also clinically described but their individual causes are not resolved; these findings are not assumed to share a mechanism.

selected_evidence.snippet:
Joint contractures, including
club feet, were present in 23 % (7/30) of patients.

assertion.prompt: In STAG2-altered Ewing sarcoma, which causal arm best explains high-risk disease: multimeric GGAA enhancer amplification, PRC2/CTCF chromatin rewiring, replication-fork repair vulnerability, or a context-specific combination of these mechanisms?
assertion.rationale:
The reviewed literature supports that STAG2 loss reshapes GGAA enhancer-promoter contacts and is clinically adverse, but the mechanism is not a single clean edge. EWS-FLI1-dependent long-GGAA contacts, EWS-FLI1- independent CTCF changes, PRC2 derepression, TP53 co-alteration, and replication-fork stress could each contribute differently across cohorts, ancestry backgrounds, and treatment states. Protein loss, mutation, enhancer occupancy and treatment sensitivity are distinct measurements.
COG diagnostic IHC/EFS and Japanese post-profiling mutation/OS results do not establish an ancestry effect. NR0B1 repeats were longer in African than European healthy subjects in PMID:22749036, the opposite of the OpenScientist cohesin report; no Japanese-repeat mechanism follows from that study. STAG2-dependent fork/HR findings from broader cancer models justify matched Ewing experiments, not a confirmed clinical predictive biomarker.

proposed_experiments.name: STAG2-stratified primary-tumor chromatin and DDR atlas
proposed_experiments.description: Profile STAG2-positive and STAG2-negative primary and relapse Ewing sarcoma specimens with matched WGS, long-read GGAA microsatellite typing, RNA-seq, ATAC-seq or CUT&Tag, H3K27ac/H3K27me3, CTCF/cohesin occupancy, and DNA-damage response markers. Pair the tumor atlas with isogenic STAG2 rescue or knockout in Ewing sarcoma cultures to separate enhancer, PRC2/CTCF, and replication-stress arms.

assertion.prompt: What GGAA microsatellite grammar and cofactor context make EWS-FLI1 binding oncogenic, and why do ETV6, BAF, and STAG2/cohesin perturbations produce different enhancer and differentiation outcomes?
assertion.rationale: EWS-FLI1 binds GGAA repeats, but binding alone does not explain why some microsatellites become oncogenic enhancers, why germline repeat length at EGR2 and RREB1 changes susceptibility, why ETV6 antagonism can redirect occupancy toward differentiation, or why STAG2 loss selectively amplifies multimeric GGAA enhancer programs. This gap is the enhancer-grammar layer of the pathograph, now spanning DNA sequence, hub dosage, native ETS competition, and cohesin state.

proposed_experiments.description: Use multiplex prime/base editing or CRISPR replacement to vary repeat length, repeat purity, flanking ETS motifs, and local chromatin context at endogenous EWS-FLI1-bound GGAA microsatellites. Combine these edits with acute BAF, ETV6, and STAG2 perturbations to quantify how enhancer grammar and cofactor state determine transcriptional output.

assertion.prompt: By what route does STAG2 loss raise EWS-FLI1 protein abundance, and does that increase feed back into the enhancer phenotype rather than merely accompanying it?
assertion.rationale: This entry curates the two ends of this link and nothing in between. The multiomic STAG2 loss-of-function study reports increased EWS-FLI1 protein abundance alongside the redistribution of fusion binding from short toward multimeric GGAA repeats, and does not account for the abundance change. Separately, the dosage node holds a regulated turnover pathway and a window whose output is non-monotonic in both directions, with TRIM8-mediated degradation as the curated mechanism keeping fusion protein within it. No study has asked whether STAG2 loss acts on that pathway. This matters for interpretation rather than completeness: if the protein rise is causal, the enhancer redistribution reported in STAG2-null cells is partly a dose effect operating through the curated window rather than a purely architectural consequence of losing cohesin-STAG2, and the two published mechanisms would not be independent. Deubiquitination is the obvious place to look, since USP19 stabilizes the fusion and its depletion lowers fusion levels, giving a manipulable step rather than an open-ended search. Measuring fusion ubiquitination, half-life, and USP19 and TRIM8 levels in isogenic STAG2 wild-type and null pairs, then holding fusion dose constant with a degron while removing STAG2, would separate the two.

selected_evidence.snippet: Constant EWS-FLI1 protein turnover is regulated by the ubiquitin proteasome system.

assertion.prompt: Which EWS-FLI1-induced DHX9/R-loop, SLFN11 fork-blocking, BRCA1, STAG2, and USP1-survivin states determine whether replication stress causes chemosensitivity, PARP/USP1/ATR inhibitor vulnerability, or survival and relapse?
assertion.rationale: Ewing sarcoma is sensitive to genotoxic chemotherapy, and EWS-FLI1 creates R-loops, replication stress, SLFN11-dependent fork blocking, and homologous-recombination defects. However, high-risk and relapsed tumors survive therapy, and it is not yet clear which molecular stress-state measurements predict response to PARP, ATR, USP1, or chemotherapy combinations.

assertion.prompt: Which EWS-FLI1-dependent chromatin-accessibility states are causal tumor dependencies rather than passenger signatures, and can an automated high-throughput chromatin assay distinguish therapeutically useful chromatin reversal from nonspecific cytotoxicity?
assertion.rationale: Ian Davis lab work showed that EWS-FLI1 retargets chromatin, creates nucleosome-depleted enhancer states, and can be assayed with automated high-throughput FAIRE. However, the therapeutic interpretation remains unresolved: a compound or degrader that reduces an Ewing chromatin signature could act by direct fusion-pathway reversal, by ETV6 or NuRD/HDAC/LSD1 modifier biology, by reduced EWS-FLI1 expression, or by general toxicity. A mechanism-resolved chromatin perturbation screen would convert this chromatin phenotype into a decision rule for prioritizing causal nodes and cloud-lab-ready follow-up experiments.

Screen annotated epigenetic compounds, targeted degraders, kinase/chemical-probe libraries, and EWS-FLI1 or ETV6 perturbation controls, then triage hits by matched viability, fusion expression, enhancer activity, and transcriptional rescue.

assertion.prompt: In STAG2-altered Ewing sarcoma, which causal arm best explains high-risk disease: multimeric GGAA enhancer amplification, PRC2/CTCF chromatin rewiring, replication-fork repair vulnerability, or a context-specific combination of these mechanisms?
assertion.rationale:
The reviewed literature supports that STAG2 loss reshapes GGAA enhancer-promoter contacts and is clinically adverse, but the mechanism is not a single clean edge. EWS-FLI1-dependent long-GGAA contacts, EWS-FLI1- independent CTCF changes, PRC2 derepression, TP53 co-alteration, and replication-fork stress could each contribute differently across cohorts, ancestry backgrounds, and treatment states. Protein loss, mutation, enhancer occupancy and treatment sensitivity are distinct measurements.
COG diagnostic IHC/EFS and Japanese post-profiling mutation/OS results do not establish an ancestry effect. NR0B1 repeats were longer in African than European healthy subjects in PMID:22749036, the opposite of the OpenScientist cohesin report; no Japanese-repeat mechanism follows from that study. STAG2-dependent fork/HR findings from broader cancer models justify matched Ewing experiments, not a confirmed clinical predictive biomarker.

value.prompt: Which human progenitor state is truly permissive for EWS-FLI1 transformation, and what chromatin or differentiation-state features distinguish transforming early mesenchymal or neural crest-like cells from non-transforming MSC states?
value.rationale:
Neural crest-derived cells, bone marrow-derived MSCs, pediatric MSCs, adult MSCs, and 2025 embryonic MSC models support overlapping but not identical origin hypotheses. The unresolved mechanism is not simply whether EWS-FLI1 can alter transcription, but which developmental chromatin state lets GGAA enhancer rewiring become transforming rather than toxic, senescent, or differentiation-inducing. IGF-1/YAP1 signaling and germline GGAA repeat architecture now provide concrete cooperating mechanisms, but neither yet defines the full permissive human progenitor state. The fusion can pioneer previously closed GGAA sites, so pre-existing accessibility at all repeats
is not a necessary criterion for permissiveness. Adult diagnosis does not by itself date the initiating event. YAP1 opposition to fusion transcription is not equivalent to tumor suppression in established Ewing sarcoma.

assertion.prompt: Does neoadjuvant denosumab increase the risk of local recurrence after subsequent curettage, and if so, is that an artefact of indication bias or a real consequence of leaving mutant stroma in a drug-induced quiescent state?
assertion.rationale: The mechanism predicts the problem. Denosumab acts on RANKL, depleting the reactive osteoclast compartment; in cell-line work it neither inhibits the growth of nor kills the neoplastic stromal cells, and it does not alter their RANKL or OPG expression. The compartment that carries the driver mutation is therefore untouched, and the new bone the drug induces may make residual tumor harder to identify and clear at surgery. Reported recurrence after denosumab-then-surgery ranges from 20% to 100% across a systematic review - a spread wide enough to be uninformative on its own, and one that could equally reflect indication bias, since the drug is given to the worst tumors. Resolving this needs a design that controls for baseline tumor severity, which no published study has.

assertion.prompt: Is the only naturally occurring animal counterpart of this disease driven by the same oncohistone, or does the canine tumor reach the same histology by a different molecular route?
assertion.rationale: The canine vertebral case reproduces the human tumor's architecture - osteoclastic giant cells evenly distributed among spindled mononuclear cells - and its destructive osteolysis, yet showed no nuclear reactivity with the H3.3 G34W mutation-specific antibody. Three readings are compatible with that result and they have different consequences. If the antibody, validated only in human tissue, simply fails to cross-react, the dog is a usable model of the human mechanism. If canine H3.3 differs in sequence context around codon 34, the species is uninformative about this driver. If canine giant cell tumors are genuinely driven by something else, then the shared histology is convergent, and the tumor's architecture is a general outcome of stromal-osteoclast cross-talk rather than a specific consequence of this oncohistone - which would be the most interesting result of the three, and would argue that the histology is not diagnostic of the mechanism. Nothing short of sequencing distinguishes them.

assertion.prompt: What inherited factor predisposes to giant cell tumor arising in Paget disease of bone, and does that subset share the H3-3A G34W driver curated for conventional sporadic GCTB?
assertion.rationale: This entry models conventional sporadic GCTB and asserts no inheritance. A distinct subset contradicts that framing at the level of the disease name, and is recorded here rather than silently dropped. Giant cell tumor arising in Paget disease clusters strongly in families, is disproportionately multifocal, favours flat bones over the long-bone epiphyses this entry describes, and carries roughly 50 percent five-year mortality against 0 to 5 percent for GCT without Paget disease. The predisposition is most plausibly inherited through Paget disease genetics rather than through anything in the mechanism graph curated here, but the retrieved literature does not establish the germline basis of the GCT phenotype specifically, and does not report whether these tumors carry H3-3A G34W at all. Until that is known it is not possible to say whether PDB-associated GCT is the same disease arising on a permissive background, or a mechanistically separate entity sharing a histological name - which is why it is scoped out of this entry rather than merged into it, and why a separate entry would be the right home for it.

assertion.prompt: Does the H3.3-G34W oncohistone initiate a giant cell tumor in vivo, and does the stromal-to-osteoclast paracrine loop operate as modeled when both compartments are present in a living skeleton?
assertion.rationale: Every mechanistic step curated in this entry between the mutation and the osteoclast compartment - the epigenetic reprogramming, the differentiation block, SCUBE3 de-repression, the SEMA4D return signal - rests on patient-derived cultures, edited tumor-derived cell lines, and monocyte co-cultures. No genetically engineered animal carrying a knock-in G34W allele was identified in this curation pass. That matters more here than in most diseases, because the central claim is specifically about cross-talk between two cell compartments: a monoculture cannot test it, and a co-culture reconstitutes it only in the absence of bone matrix, vasculature, and an intact recruitment step. The tumor-formation experiment that establishes necessity was performed in cells that were already tumor-derived, so initiation from a normal mesenchymal progenitor remains untested.

value.prompt: Is the only naturally occurring animal counterpart of this disease driven by the same oncohistone, or does the canine tumor reach the same histology by a different molecular route?
value.rationale: The canine vertebral case reproduces the human tumor's architecture - osteoclastic giant cells evenly distributed among spindled mononuclear cells - and its destructive osteolysis, yet showed no nuclear reactivity with the H3.3 G34W mutation-specific antibody. Three readings are compatible with that result and they have different consequences. If the antibody, validated only in human tissue, simply fails to cross-react, the dog is a usable model of the human mechanism. If canine H3.3 differs in sequence context around codon 34, the species is uninformative about this driver. If canine giant cell tumors are genuinely driven by something else, then the shared histology is convergent, and the tumor's architecture is a general outcome of stromal-osteoclast cross-talk rather than a specific consequence of this oncohistone - which would be the most interesting result of the three, and would argue that the histology is not diagnostic of the mechanism. Nothing short of sequencing distinguishes them.

value.name: Targeted sequencing of H3-3A codon 34 in canine giant cell tumors
value.description: Sequence the H3-3A codon 34 region in a series of canine giant cell bone tumors, alongside alignment of the canine H3.3 epitope against the human sequence the antibody was raised to, to separate assay failure from true molecular divergence.

assertion.interpretation: Absence of any codon 34 change with a conserved epitope would establish genuine divergence; presence with a negative stain would establish assay failure. Direction is recorded as UNCHANGED because the informative result is the wild-type one.

assertion.prompt: Does neoadjuvant denosumab increase the risk of local recurrence after subsequent curettage, and if so, is that an artefact of indication bias or a real consequence of leaving mutant stroma in a drug-induced quiescent state?
assertion.rationale: The mechanism predicts the problem. Denosumab acts on RANKL, depleting the reactive osteoclast compartment; in cell-line work it neither inhibits the growth of nor kills the neoplastic stromal cells, and it does not alter their RANKL or OPG expression. The compartment that carries the driver mutation is therefore untouched, and the new bone the drug induces may make residual tumor harder to identify and clear at surgery. Reported recurrence after denosumab-then-surgery ranges from 20% to 100% across a systematic review - a spread wide enough to be uninformative on its own, and one that could equally reflect indication bias, since the drug is given to the worst tumors. Resolving this needs a design that controls for baseline tumor severity, which no published study has.

selected_evidence.snippet: Our findings provide new insights in the anti-tumor effect of denosumab on GCT stromal cells and raise a concern that tumor recurrence may occur after the withdrawal of the drug.

assertion.prompt: Is CBP physically depleted from the nucleus into polyglutamine aggregates in Huntington disease, or is it present at normal levels and functionally inhibited by soluble mutant huntingtin? Two bodies of work on the same protein reach opposite answers, and the therapeutic implication differs: clearing aggregates versus disrupting a soluble protein-protein interaction.
assertion.rationale: Both sides are experimentally serious and neither is obviously wrong. The depletion side has cross-system concordance (cell culture, transgenic mice, human postmortem brain) plus a single-cell result in which CBP loss, histone hypo-acetylation and toxicity travel together and are all reversed by CBP overexpression. The no-depletion side tested the model four ways in HD mouse brain, found CBP diffusely nuclear despite abundant inclusions, showed most CBP not co-localized with inclusions by double labelling and electron microscopy, and confirmed by western blot that it was not trapped. The likely reconciliation is that the two are measuring different things: transfected single cells with high mutant huntingtin expression versus whole mouse brain, and functional availability versus total protein. That reconciliation is plausible but untested, which is why this is recorded as a controversy rather than resolved in favour of either. The wider mechanism is not in doubt in the same way. TBP deactivation by soluble oligomers is demonstrated with a chaperone rescue, and the entry's description has been written around functional inhibition accordingly; what remains open is specifically whether CBP is additionally lost from the nucleus.

proposed_experiments.name: CBP abundance against H3K27ac occupancy in graded human HD striatum
proposed_experiments.description: In postmortem HD caudate spanning early and late Vonsattel grades with matched controls, measure total and nuclear CBP protein alongside genome-wide H3K27ac, the mark CBP deposits. Physical depletion and functional inhibition make different predictions that can be told apart in one experiment: depletion predicts reduced CBP protein with globally reduced H3K27ac, whereas functional inhibition predicts preserved CBP protein with H3K27ac lost selectively at mutant-huntingtin-sensitive loci. Running it in human tissue also removes the confound that the existing disagreement may rest on transfected cells versus whole mouse brain.

assertion.prompt: Somatic CAG expansion is the rate-limiting upstream event in HD, and extrasynaptic NMDAR redistribution is the proximate lesion of the excitotoxicity hypothesis, but no experiment has connected them. Does blocking somatic expansion prevent the synaptic-to-extrasynaptic GluN2B shift?
assertion.rationale: The two mechanisms are routinely described as sequential - expansion raises the effective polyQ length, which then disrupts receptor trafficking - but the ordering is asserted rather than demonstrated. Msh3 deletion in Q140 mice abolishes somatic expansion and corrects synaptic and locomotor defects, yet the published readouts do not include compartment-resolved NMDAR localization, so the two mechanisms could equally be parallel consequences of the inherited allele. Which it is decides whether somatic-expansion suppression alone should be expected to normalize excitotoxic vulnerability, or whether the two need separate interventions. The experiment is a straightforward addition to an existing cross rather than new model construction.

proposed_experiments.name: Extrasynaptic NMDAR measurement in expansion-incompetent HD knock-in mice
proposed_experiments.description: Cross Msh3-null mice onto a Q140 or YAC128 background and measure the extrasynaptic/synaptic NMDAR current ratio by whole-cell patch clamp in acute striatal slices, alongside GluN2B surface distribution, at ages spanning the presymptomatic window. Compare against expansion-competent littermates matched for inherited repeat length, so the only variable is whether the tract grew.

readouts.name: Extrasynaptic to synaptic NMDAR current ratio
readouts.description: Whole-cell NMDAR current partitioned into synaptic and extrasynaptic components in medium spiny neurons of expansion-competent and expansion-incompetent animals.

readouts.name: Striatal somatic CAG repeat length
readouts.description: Confirms that the Msh3-null arm did in fact hold repeat length at the inherited value in the neurons being recorded from.

controls.name: Expansion-competent HD knock-in littermates
controls.description: Same inherited repeat length, intact mismatch repair.

controls.name: Msh3-null wild-type littermates
controls.description: Controls for any effect of Msh3 loss on NMDAR trafficking itself.

proposed_experiments.decision_criterion: The sequential model is supported if the extrasynaptic/synaptic ratio in Msh3-null HD mice is normalized toward wild type in proportion to the blocked expansion. It is not supported if the ratio shifts as much as in expansion-competent animals, which would make redistribution a parallel consequence of the inherited allele.
supporting_outcome: Normalized extrasynaptic NMDAR current in expansion-incompetent animals despite unchanged inherited repeat length.
refuting_outcome: An unchanged extrasynaptic shift in animals whose CAG tract never grew.

assertion.prompt: Mitochondrial deficit in HD has two arms, reduced biogenesis through PGC-1alpha repression and reduced clearance through disrupted mitophagy, but their relative contributions to the net deficit have never been measured against each other. Which arm dominates, and does it differ by cell type or disease stage?
assertion.rationale: The two arms have been studied independently and never in the same preparation, so the question has no answer rather than a contested one. It matters because the therapeutic strategies diverge completely: PGC-1alpha activation for a biogenesis-limited deficit, mitophagy induction for a clearance-limited one, and the failure of untargeted bioenergetic supplementation in HD is a reason to want the distinction before designing the next trial. The measurement is tractable - simultaneous turnover reporters in isogenic human neurons - and does not need new model construction.

proposed_experiments.name: Paired mitochondrial biogenesis and mitophagy flux in isogenic HD striatal neurons
proposed_experiments.description: Use mito-Keima or MitoTimer reporters in HD iPSC-derived striatal neurons and their isogenic CAG-corrected controls to measure mitophagy flux and organelle age distribution in the same cells, alongside mitochondrial mass and PGC-1alpha target expression. Perturb each arm separately - PGC-1alpha overexpression against mitophagy induction - and compare how much of the mitochondrial content and respiratory deficit each recovers.

model_systems.name: Isogenic HD iPSC-derived striatal projection neuron model
model_systems.description: Patient-derived and CAG-corrected striatal neurons carrying live mitochondrial turnover reporters, so production and clearance can be read in the same cell.

perturbations.name: PGC-1alpha restoration
perturbations.description: Overexpression of PGC-1alpha to test the biogenesis arm in isolation.

perturbations.name: Mitophagy induction
perturbations.description: Pharmacological or PINK1/Parkin-driven enhancement of mitophagy to test the clearance arm in isolation.

readouts.name: Mitophagy flux
readouts.description: Rate of delivery of mitochondria to lysosomes, read from the reporter's pH-dependent signal.

readouts.name: Mitochondrial mass and respiratory capacity
readouts.description: Net organelle content and oxygen consumption rate in the same cultures, so each perturbation's rescue can be attributed to its arm.

controls.name: Isogenic CAG-corrected striatal neurons
controls.description: Same genetic background with a nonpathogenic HTT CAG tract.

proposed_experiments.decision_criterion: Whichever single-arm perturbation recovers more of the respiratory deficit identifies the rate-limiting arm. Roughly equal partial rescue with additive combined rescue would mean neither arm is limiting alone and the deficit is genuinely two-sided.
supporting_outcome: A clear asymmetry between the two single-arm rescues, identifying which process limits mitochondrial content in HD striatal neurons.
refuting_outcome: Neither perturbation changes mitochondrial content or respiration, which would place the deficit downstream of both turnover arms.

selected_evidence.snippet: HTT is involved in different mitophagy steps, promoting the physical proximity of different protein complexes during the initiation of mitophagy and recruiting mitophagy receptors essential for promoting the interaction between damaged mitochondria and the nascent autophagosome.

assertion.prompt: Mitochondrial deficit in HD has two arms, reduced biogenesis through PGC-1alpha repression and reduced clearance through disrupted mitophagy, but their relative contributions to the net deficit have never been measured against each other. Which arm dominates, and does it differ by cell type or disease stage?
assertion.rationale: The two arms have been studied independently and never in the same preparation, so the question has no answer rather than a contested one. It matters because the therapeutic strategies diverge completely: PGC-1alpha activation for a biogenesis-limited deficit, mitophagy induction for a clearance-limited one, and the failure of untargeted bioenergetic supplementation in HD is a reason to want the distinction before designing the next trial. The measurement is tractable - simultaneous turnover reporters in isogenic human neurons - and does not need new model construction.

proposed_experiments.name: Paired mitochondrial biogenesis and mitophagy flux in isogenic HD striatal neurons
proposed_experiments.description: Use mito-Keima or MitoTimer reporters in HD iPSC-derived striatal neurons and their isogenic CAG-corrected controls to measure mitophagy flux and organelle age distribution in the same cells, alongside mitochondrial mass and PGC-1alpha target expression. Perturb each arm separately - PGC-1alpha overexpression against mitophagy induction - and compare how much of the mitochondrial content and respiratory deficit each recovers.

model_systems.name: Isogenic HD iPSC-derived striatal projection neuron model
model_systems.description: Patient-derived and CAG-corrected striatal neurons carrying live mitochondrial turnover reporters, so production and clearance can be read in the same cell.

perturbations.name: PGC-1alpha restoration
perturbations.description: Overexpression of PGC-1alpha to test the biogenesis arm in isolation.

perturbations.name: Mitophagy induction
perturbations.description: Pharmacological or PINK1/Parkin-driven enhancement of mitophagy to test the clearance arm in isolation.

readouts.name: Mitophagy flux
readouts.description: Rate of delivery of mitochondria to lysosomes, read from the reporter's pH-dependent signal.

readouts.name: Mitochondrial mass and respiratory capacity
readouts.description: Net organelle content and oxygen consumption rate in the same cultures, so each perturbation's rescue can be attributed to its arm.

controls.name: Isogenic CAG-corrected striatal neurons
controls.description: Same genetic background with a nonpathogenic HTT CAG tract.

proposed_experiments.decision_criterion: Whichever single-arm perturbation recovers more of the respiratory deficit identifies the rate-limiting arm. Roughly equal partial rescue with additive combined rescue would mean neither arm is limiting alone and the deficit is genuinely two-sided.
supporting_outcome: A clear asymmetry between the two single-arm rescues, identifying which process limits mitochondrial content in HD striatal neurons.
refuting_outcome: Neither perturbation changes mitochondrial content or respiration, which would place the deficit downstream of both turnover arms.

selected_evidence.snippet: Studies over the past few years have implicated an impaired function of peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor (PPAR)-gamma coactivator-1alpha (PGC-1alpha), a transcriptional master coregulator of mitochondrial biogenesis, metabolism, and antioxidant defenses, in causing mitochondrial dysfunction in HD.

assertion.prompt: Every direct measurement of the synaptic-to-extrasynaptic GluN2B shift that the excitotoxicity hypothesis rests on comes from mouse models. In human HD the available signals point the other way: postmortem NMDAR subunit mRNA falls with disease severity and the astrocytic glutamate-transporter response reads as compensatory, HD onset-modifier GWAS return mismatch-repair genes and no glutamate-receptor-pathway signal, and NMDA receptor antagonists have failed advanced trials. Does extrasynaptic NMDAR redistribution operate in human HD brain, or is it a property of the mouse models?
assertion.rationale: This is a mismatch rather than a plain evidence gap: the mouse evidence is strong, mechanistic and interventional, and the human evidence exists but does not obviously agree with it. The three human observations are individually weak arguments - subunit mRNA loss is expected from neuronal loss, absence of a genome-wide significant modifier signal is weak evidence of no effect for a mechanism that may act downstream of onset, and pan-NMDAR blockade removes physiological signalling along with pathological signalling - but they point the same way, and none of them is what the mouse work predicts. The measurement that would settle it does not exist: no PET ligand distinguishes synaptic from extrasynaptic NMDA receptors, so the compartment claim cannot be tested in living human brain at all. Until it can, extrasynaptic redistribution should be curated as a mouse mechanism with a plausible but unconfirmed human counterpart, and the excitotoxicity hypothesis should stay ALTERNATIVE.

proposed_experiments.name: Compartment-resolved NMDA receptor profiling across human HD Vonsattel grades
proposed_experiments.description: Take postmortem striatum spanning Vonsattel grades 0-4 with age-matched controls, fractionate synaptic and extrasynaptic membrane compartments, and quantify GluN2B content, GluN2B S1303 and Y1472 phosphorylation, and calpain-cleaved GluN2B in each compartment. Pair with spatial transcriptomics so receptor distribution can be read against surviving medium spiny neuron density rather than against bulk tissue. The prediction from the mouse work is that the extrasynaptic fraction rises earliest, before neuronal loss, and that the S1303 and calpain-cleavage marks track it.

model_systems.name: Human HD postmortem striatum series

readouts.name: Extrasynaptic versus synaptic GluN2B content
readouts.description: GluN2B abundance in biochemically separated synaptic and extrasynaptic membrane fractions, expressed as a ratio so it is not confounded by overall receptor loss.

readouts.name: Surviving medium spiny neuron density by grade
readouts.description: Neuronal density in the same blocks, used to establish whether any compartment shift precedes or merely accompanies cell loss.

controls.name: Age-matched non-neurological controls
controls.description: Postmortem striatum with matched interval and fixation handling.

controls.name: Non-HD neurodegenerative comparator
controls.description: A second neurodegenerative striatal pathology, to test whether any shift is specific to HD rather than a generic consequence of degeneration.

proposed_experiments.decision_criterion: The human counterpart is supported if the extrasynaptic/synaptic GluN2B ratio is elevated at grades 0-1, before substantial neuronal loss, and declines thereafter. supporting_outcome: An early, pre-degenerative rise in the extrasynaptic GluN2B fraction that is absent from the non-HD comparator.
refuting_outcome: An extrasynaptic fraction that is unchanged or falls in proportion to surviving neurons across all grades.

selected_evidence.snippet: For this reason many NMDA receptor antagonists have disappointingly failed advanced clinical trials for a number of diseases including stroke and neurodegenerative disorders such as Huntington's disease.

assertion.prompt: Does the somatic-CAG-expansion therapeutic rationale, which underpins MSH3- and FAN1-directed programmes in adult-onset HD, still apply in the juvenile repeat range, where the inherited allele may already exceed the pathogenic threshold and further somatic expansion may be dispensable for pathogenesis?
assertion.rationale: In the zQ175 knock-in model, whose approximately 185-CAG allele sits in the juvenile/pediatric rather than adult range, complete Msh3 ablation abolished somatic expansion throughout brain and periphery and 50% reduction slowed it - yet neither striatal nuclear huntingtin aggregation nor the dysregulated striatal transcriptional profile improved. This is the opposite of the result obtained when Msh3 is ablated in knock-in models carrying shorter, adult-range repeats, where the intervention is beneficial. The authors' own translational argument is that human repeats of comparable size cause onset before age 2, so somatic expansion in brain cannot be required for pathogenesis at these lengths. The mismatch is therefore two-sided and specifically juvenile. Model-to-human: the negative result is a mouse result, and no trial of somatic-instability-directed therapy has been run in children with juvenile-onset HD - they are excluded from most HD trials, so the human counterpart of this experiment does not exist. Human-to-model: the repeat length at which the benefit of somatic-expansion suppression disappears is unknown in humans, because the trajectory of somatic expansion in mutation-carrier brain has not been measured. Until that threshold is located, an MSH3- or FAN1-directed agent validated in adult-onset HD must not be assumed to transfer to juvenile-onset patients, and the practical implication the authors draw - treat as early as possible, before the threshold is crossed - is itself untested in this group. This discussion deliberately does not resolve the general somatic-expansion gap recorded in gap_hd_somatic_expansion_threshold_rescue; it is the juvenile-range special case of it, where the sign of the expected effect may differ.

proposed_experiments.name: Repeat-length-titrated MSH3 suppression in juvenile-range HD neurons
proposed_experiments.description: Locate the repeat length at which suppressing somatic expansion stops conferring benefit, using isogenic human striatal neurons spanning the adult-onset through juvenile and highly expanded pediatric ranges. Apply graded MSH3 knockdown to each line, then measure somatic expansion alongside the phenotypes that failed to respond in zQ175 - nuclear huntingtin aggregation and the striatal transcriptional signature - plus survival. The read-out of interest is not whether suppression works at any one length but where in the repeat-length series the dose-response inverts, which is the number needed to decide whether juvenile-onset patients belong in MSH3-directed trials at all.

model_systems.name: Juvenile-range isogenic hPSC-derived striatal neuron allelic series
model_systems.description: Human pluripotent-stem-cell-derived striatal projection neurons carrying an isogenic series of HTT CAG tract lengths that spans the adult-onset, juvenile, and highly expanded pediatric ranges, so repeat length is the only variable distinguishing the lines.

selected_evidence.snippet: Ablation of Msh3 prevented somatic expansion throughout the brain and periphery, and reduction of Msh3 by 50% decreased the rate of expansion.

assertion.prompt: Do accumulating double-strand breaks cause the transcriptional dysfunction seen in HD striatal neurons - through error-prone end-joining variants and transcription blockade at unrepaired breaks - or do the two simply arise in parallel from mutant huntingtin?
assertion.rationale: The source study is explicit that this was not tested: double-strand break accumulation was shown to coincide with transcriptional dysfunction in both zQ175 and zQ175/MSH3(-/-) mice regardless of somatic expansion, but no experiment established the causal direction. The authors also note a tension in their own model - transcriptional changes in HD are reproducible between studies, which is difficult to derive from breaks distributed at random across the genome. Their proposed resolution is that repair at preferred sites (clustered single-strand breaks at neuronal gene enhancers, where SAR-seq peaks co-localise with PARP and XRCC1) yields recurrent variants while random breaks elsewhere contribute undetectably. The edge from Genome-Wide Double Strand Break Accumulation to Transcriptional Dysregulation is therefore curated with causal_link_type INDIRECT_UNKNOWN_INTERMEDIATES and PARTIAL evidence.

proposed_experiments.name: Temporal ordering of break burden and transcriptome change
proposed_experiments.description: Dense time-course sampling of matched striatal tissue for break markers and RNA-seq in HdhQ(150/150) mice, testing whether break burden rises before the transcriptional signature diverges.

proposed_experiments.name: Break suppression as a transcriptome intervention
proposed_experiments.description: Repeat the XJB-5-131 late-start regimen with striatal RNA-seq as the primary endpoint, testing whether lowering break burden corrects the transcriptional signature and not only neuron number and motor score.

proposed_experiments.name: Map repair junctions against dysregulated genes
proposed_experiments.description: Sequence end-joining repair junctions genome-wide in aged disease striatum and test whether somatic variants are enriched at the regulatory elements of the genes that are transcriptionally dysregulated, as the clustered-SSB hypothesis predicts.

selected_evidence.snippet: DSBs and transcriptional dysfunction occur in animals that cannot somatically expand their inherited allele.

assertion.prompt: Which mechanisms account for early metabolic and feeding findings?
assertion.rationale: The infant report establishes neonatal acidosis, hypoglycemia and feeding difficulty, with transient hyperammonemia in Patient 2 and hypothermia in Patient 1. A qualified OXPHOS-to-lactic-acidosis route is represented using established pyruvate/redox physiology and the MRPL44 clinical measurements; missing tissue-level reconstruction does not negate that relation. The precise tissue contribution and possible cardiac/illness amplification remain unresolved. Intrinsic hypoglycemia, hypothermia, hyperammonemia and feeding difficulty are less causally localized by these sources. Hypoglycemia preceded cardiac shock; the shock link concerns its acute exacerbation only. Feeding insufficiency has a supported nutritional route to poor growth. Patient 1 also carried a 16q23.3 deletion. No blanket ATP-depletion fanout is asserted.

assertion.prompt: Can the yeast MrpL3/mL44 homolog or a mouse Mrpl44 knockout serve as a valid model for human MRPL44 disease alleles, given that the human disease mutation modelled at the equivalent yeast residue does not impair function and that mouse null loss is embryonically lethal?
attaches_to: pathophysiology#Biallelic MRPL44 Loss of Function and mL44 Protein Depletion
assertion.rationale: Yeast MrpL3/mL44 is the tractable genetic model for mL44 function, and mutagenesis of its conserved hydrophobic pocket does identify residues critical for assembling translationally active mitoribosomes. However, the exact human disease substitution modelled at the equivalent yeast residue (A186) had no major functional impact, and the authors concluded the two orthologs have diverged in evolution. Mouse Mrpl44 loss is a different kind of mismatch: knockout is embryonically lethal, whereas human patients carry hypomorphic alleles with residual protein and survive with tissue-restricted disease. Neither model therefore reproduces the human hypomorphic, cardiac-selective genotype-phenotype relationship, and both should be treated as tools for general mitoribosome biology rather than as MRPL44 disease models. Patient-derived iPSC cardiomyocytes are the emerging replacement, but the only published line covers a single genotype and the work remains a preprint.

proposed_experiments.name: Isogenic MRPL44 iPSC-derived cardiomyocyte allelic series
proposed_experiments.description: Engineer an allelic series (p.Leu156Arg, p.Leu156Pro, p.Thr161Serfs*2, and corrected wild type) in a common human iPSC background, differentiate to cardiomyocytes, and quantify mL44 abundance, 39S assembly, mitochondrial translation, complex I and IV activity, and contractile function, testing whether the human cardiac context reproduces the allele-severity gradient that neither yeast nor mouse captures.

model_systems.description: Cardiomyocytes differentiated from gene-edited human iPSCs carrying the reported MRPL44 disease alleles, preserving the human sequence context that diverges from yeast MrpL3.

assertion.prompt: What determines the striking tissue gradient of MRPL44 deficiency, in which heart muscle shows profound respiratory chain deficiency, skeletal muscle intermediate, and fibroblasts only borderline changes, despite comparable reduction of mL44 protein in all three tissues?
assertion.rationale: mL44 protein levels are reduced in heart, skeletal muscle, and fibroblasts alike, yet the enzymatic and clinical consequences are overwhelmingly cardiac. Candidate explanations include the higher OXPHOS flux demand and mitochondrial density of the myocardium, the postnatal switch to fatty-acid oxidation (the nutrient-dependent hypothesis), tissue-specific differences in mitoribosome assembly-factor buffering, and a possible transcript hierarchy in mitochondrial translation - the yeast work showed that MrpL3/mL44 mutation does not affect all mtDNA-encoded transcripts equally. Distinguishing a threshold effect from a genuinely cardiac-specific mechanism is required before extrapolating any therapy tested in fibroblasts to the heart.

selected_evidence.snippet: There are tissue specific differences. The enzyme deficiency was most pronounced in cardiac muscle tissue, where there was massive proliferation of mitochondria on electron microscopy displacing contractile elements.

assertion.prompt: Which tissue-specific mechanisms explain the remaining clinical manifestations in clinically defined MELAS?
assertion.rationale: The remaining clinical gaps have distinct evidence limitations. GeneReviews supports migraine as a possible trigger of stroke-like episodes, now represented in that direction; it does not establish the cause of migraine or a reverse cortical-injury-to-migraine relation. Short stature and learning disability are documented clinically, but the reviewed sources do not identify a phenotype-specific causal relation from the curated mechanisms; learning disability is not interchangeable with acquired dementia. The m.3243A>G cohort documents MELAS/PEO overlap without establishing the causal sequence from generalized myopathy to extraocular dysfunction. The ptosis case provides occurrence evidence, including a prior myasthenia diagnosis, without establishing eyelid-muscle pathogenesis. Broad conduction abnormalities, right bundle branch block, and Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome are documented, but the reviewed sources do not establish their causal route from the curated myocardial remodeling mechanism or explain how mitochondrial dysfunction produces an accessory conduction pathway. The anemia cohort explicitly leaves dietary and other contributors unresolved. The imaging study documents cerebellar atrophy and basal ganglia calcification but does not establish their causal route from the cortical stroke-like lesion mechanism. Its suggestion of dystrophic calcification does not identify the initiating injury. Lactate, ragged-red fibers, and focal epileptiform EEG discharges are linked separately as observational readouts. GeneReviews documents ataxia without assigning it to the cortical injury mechanism or establishing that the imaged cerebellar atrophy causes it. The cardiac review supports a qualified remodeling-to-arrhythmia relation, now represented, but the right bundle branch block case is not causally assigned to that remodeling route by the observational cohort. These gaps concern causal attribution, not a requirement to identify every intermediate step.

assertion.prompt: Which cardiac findings reported across m.3243A>G carriers can be assigned specifically to clinically defined MELAS?

assertion.prompt: Why does one variant, m.3243A>G, produce MELAS in some carriers, MIDD or isolated deafness in others, and nothing at all in a further group?
assertion.rationale:
Only about 10% of m.3243A>G carriers in a systematically phenotyped cohort had classical MELAS, while 30% had MIDD, 28% had a combination fitting no recognized syndrome, and 9% were asymptomatic. Heteroplasmy level is the conventional explanation, but measured heteroplasmy explains far less than it is credited with: it did not correlate with disease severity in leukocytes or urinary epithelial cells, and it did not correlate with the grade of retinal dystrophy either. Tissue-specific segregation, nuclear genetic background, mtDNA copy number, and age are all candidate modifiers, and none has been shown to account for the variance. This is what makes genetic counselling and prognosis in m.3243A>G families so weak.
Four public datasets attached here attack the gap from different angles and are worth reading against each other. GSE202747 measures heteroplasmy per cell in a human MELAS tissue and finds it partitions by developmental lineage rather than randomly, which would make any single bulk measurement a poor proxy. GSE56158 varies heteroplasmy experimentally in one nuclear background and finds sharp transcriptional transitions rather than a gradient, offering a mechanism by which a continuous variable yields named syndromes. GSE129091 compares low against high load directly on the MELAS-versus-MIDD axis and reports that the two look alike transcriptionally while differing functionally. GSE85549 moves the question from heteroplasmy to allele, comparing the MELAS m.3243A>G lesion against the myopathy-causing m.3302A>G in the same gene. MSV000088237 extends the allele question outside MT-TL1 entirely, profiling fibroblasts from a patient with the complex I subunit variant m.14453G>A. GSE1462 is the only one that holds genotype constant and varies phenotype in patients - four PEO against four MELAS, all m.3243A>G, all muscle - and its authors read the difference as support for nuclear background as the modifier. That is the right experimental design for this gap, at a sample size and on a 2005 platform that cannot settle it.

assertion.prompt: How much of the MELAS phenotype outside the nervous system is genuinely absent versus simply not looked for?
assertion.rationale: Three organ systems are described in their own literatures as under-recognized in m.3243A>G disease. Renal involvement is called probably underestimated; oligosymptomatic and kidney-limited m.3243A>G presentations can be difficult to recognize. Intestinal pseudo-obstruction is under-recognized and can be the presenting problem. Cardiac involvement has rarely been studied prospectively, which the reviewers themselves offer as the reason its reported incidence looks lower than expected. GeneReviews provides syndrome-level frequency intervals for cardiomyopathy, conduction abnormalities, and nephropathy. The 2025 cardiac study supplies a right-bundle-branch-block denominator among 11 clinical MELAS participants, but participation from 30 contacted patients was limited by severity and deaths. Neither those results nor the GeneReviews intervals close the separate ascertainment gap in unselected m.3243A>G carriers. This is the one gap in the entry that omics deposits cannot close, because it is a sampling problem rather than a mechanistic one - and a survey of public repositories bore that out, returning no dataset that changes the denominator. The relevant public resources are instead the two natural-history efforts attached here: NCT01532791, which recruits through maternal relatives of known carriers regardless of their own carrier status and uses paternal relatives as controls, and NCT05554835, which harmonizes national registries into a global cohort. A related class-level resource, Metabolomics Workbench study ST003924, profiles urinary metabolites in genetically confirmed paediatric primary mitochondrial disorders with an explicitly renal framing, but its sample factors record only the disease-class label, so MELAS cases cannot be identified within it and it is deliberately not curated as a MELAS dataset here.

value.prompt: Are mast cells a causal upstream driver of blood-brain-barrier disruption and microglial neuroinflammation in Long COVID brain fog, or are mast-cell signatures a downstream marker of broader immune activation?
value.rationale: The current evidence is mechanistically compelling but largely cellular and associative. A human neurovascular model with controlled mast-cell activation would test whether mast cells are sufficient and necessary for barrier dysfunction and microglial activation under SARS-CoV-2-relevant stimuli.

assertion.name: Laser-bioprinted human neurovascular organ-on-chip mast-cell activation assay
assertion.description: Use BioLP/LIFT-style biological laser printing to pattern a human blood-brain-barrier organ-on-chip containing brain microvascular endothelium, mural support cells, microglia, and mast cells; expose it to SARS-CoV-2 spike or Long-COVID patient serum; then test whether mast-cell stabilization or antihistamine blockade prevents barrier leak and microglial inflammatory activation.

model_systems.name: Laser-bioprinted human neurovascular blood-brain-barrier organ-on-chip
model_systems.description: Microfluidic human neurovascular unit model fabricated by high-resolution biological laser printing so endothelial and support cells can be placed in reproducible vascular geometries for barrier permeability and immune-cell-mediated neuroinflammation assays.
model_systems.notes: Highlights Bradley R. Ringeisen's BioLP/LIFT lineage: an orifice-free laser-printing modality for precise living-cell deposition that can be adapted to standardized neurovascular-chip fabrication.

perturbations.name: SARS-CoV-2 spike exposure
perturbations.description: Spike-protein exposure or patient-serum challenge used to trigger mast-cell activation in the neurovascular model.

perturbations.name: Mast-cell stabilization or histamine blockade
perturbations.description: Pharmacologic suppression of mast-cell mediator release or histamine signaling to test necessity of mast-cell activation.

readouts.name: Blood-brain-barrier permeability
readouts.description: Barrier leak and endothelial inflammatory-state readouts interpreted as upstream permissive events for neuroinflammation.

readouts.name: Microglial inflammatory activation
readouts.description: Cytokine and microglial-state readouts after mast-cell activation.
readouts.interpretation: Reduced microglial activation after mast-cell stabilization would support mast cells as an upstream, targetable driver.

controls.name: Mast-cell-absent neurovascular chip
controls.description: Matched neurovascular chip lacking mast cells to test necessity.

controls.name: Healthy-control serum exposure
controls.description: Matched serum exposure from healthy controls.

assertion.decision_criterion: Mast-cell activation is supported as causal if SARS-CoV-2-relevant challenge increases barrier permeability and microglial activation, and these readouts are reduced in mast-cell-absent or mast-cell-stabilized conditions.
assertion.notes: BioLP/LIFT is used here as a TA3-style instrument-defined fabrication protocol, complementary to hPSC genome-engineering examples: it specifies where living cells are placed, enabling a repeatable TA4 assay surface for barrier and neuroimmune readouts.
