attaches_to: pathophysiology#Disrupted Brain Development and Structural Malformation
assertion.prompt: Why do humans with biallelic CSF1R loss of function develop severe congenital brain malformations while Csf1r knockout rats, which lack microglia just as completely, undergo essentially normal brain development?
assertion.rationale: The rat Csf1rko removes the entire microglial population - the same cellular lesion documented at autopsy in BANDDOS - yet diffusion imaging and region-wise RNA-seq show only small fibre-tract reductions and no neuronal or regional transcriptomic change, and the authors conclude that most brain developmental processes occur normally without microglia. Human biallelic CSF1R brains instead show callosal agenesis, Dandy-Walker complex, heterotopia, and non-decussating pyramidal tracts. The same paper concludes that CSF1R haploinsufficiency is unlikely to cause leukoencephalopathy, which is directly at odds with the established human monoallelic CSF1R-ALSP disorder. Either microglia have human-specific developmental roles (the CUX1-positive upper-layer neuron route proposed from the zebrafish and human tissue work is one candidate), or the human phenotype depends on something other than microglial absence per se. Until this is resolved, rodent rescue data cannot be read as predicting that restoring myeloid cells will correct the malformation arm of BANDDOS.

proposed_experiments.name: Human cerebral organoid or xenotransplant model with biallelic CSF1R loss
proposed_experiments.description: Compare corpus callosum-relevant projection neuron specification (CUX1-positive upper-layer neurons) in human iPSC-derived cortical systems with and without CSF1R-competent microglia, using patient-derived biallelic CSF1R lines, to test whether the developmental requirement is human-specific.

proposed_experiments.name: Developmental staging of the rodent versus human microglial requirement
proposed_experiments.description: Determine whether the discrepancy reflects the timing of microglial colonisation relative to commissural axon guidance, by comparing microglial colonisation windows and callosal pathfinding in rat, zebrafish, and human fetal tissue.

selected_evidence.snippet: We conclude that most brain developmental processes occur normally in the absence of microglia and that CSF1R haploinsufficiency is unlikely to cause leukoencephalopathy.

attaches_to: treatments#Allogeneic Hematopoietic Stem Cell Transplantation (investigational in BANDDOS)
assertion.prompt: Does hematopoietic stem cell transplantation modify the course of BANDDOS, and is there a therapeutic window before the degenerative phase begins?
assertion.rationale: HSCT is now offered in CSF1R-ALSP, and the review literature explicitly proposes translating it to BANDDOS on the basis of a shared pathomechanism. But no outcome data exist in genetically confirmed BANDDOS. Two features of BANDDOS complicate the extrapolation: the congenital malformations are already established at birth and cannot plausibly be reversed by any myeloid replacement, and in the Csf1rko rat the brain was the one organ where donor-derived cells did not transcriptionally match resident microglia. A meaningful trial would therefore have to specify which arm of the disease it expects to modify.

proposed_experiments.name: International BANDDOS natural history registry with prospective HSCT arm
proposed_experiments.description: Pool the very small worldwide case population into a registry capturing genotype, residual CSF1R function, serial MRI, and neurodevelopmental outcome, and follow any transplanted patients prospectively against untransplanted controls, with the degenerative (not developmental) arm as the pre-specified endpoint.

selected_evidence.snippet: The exception was the brain, where BM-derived microglia-like cells had a distinct expression profile compared to resident microglia.

assertion.prompt: Why does profound CSF1R deficiency spare peripheral immune function in BANDDOS patients?
assertion.rationale: CSF1R is the master regulator of the mononuclear phagocyte system, and the Csf1rko rat has a broad myeloid deficit with granulocytosis, B cell deficiency, and failure to thrive. Yet detailed immunological workup of a BANDDOS family found normal blood markers, monocytes, dendritic cell subsets, and T cell proliferation, and no clinical immunodeficiency has been reported. Whether this reflects the hypomorphic nature of human alleles, redundancy with CSF2/IL-34 signalling in the periphery, or simply incomplete phenotyping across the small case population is unresolved, and it matters for how aggressively transplant conditioning would be justified.

proposed_experiments.name: Systematic immunophenotyping across the BANDDOS case population
proposed_experiments.description: Apply uniform deep immunophenotyping (tissue-resident macrophage compartments, monocyte subsets, circulating CSF1 concentration) across reported BANDDOS patients and their heterozygous relatives, correlated with allele-specific residual CSF1R signalling measured in vitro.

selected_evidence.snippet: Despite the role of CSF1R signaling in myeloid development, immune deficiency is absent.

assertion.prompt: Is the optic atrophy of BANDDOS compressive (optic canal narrowing by craniofacial osteosclerosis) or a primary neurodegenerative process?
assertion.rationale: Optic nerve atrophy occurs in about 29% of BANDDOS cases and is not a feature of adult-onset CSF1R-ALSP, so it cannot simply be attributed to the shared leukoencephalopathy. Two candidate mechanisms exist and have opposite management implications: optic canal narrowing is a recognised element of the BANDDOS skeletal phenotype and, in other sclerosing bone dysplasias, compresses the nerve in a surgically decompressible way; alternatively the atrophy could be part of the congenital or degenerative CNS disease itself. No published BANDDOS case establishes which applies, so this entry deliberately draws no causal edge to this phenotype.

proposed_experiments.name: Optic canal imaging correlated with optic nerve structure and function
proposed_experiments.description: In reported and new BANDDOS patients, pair dedicated skull-base CT measurement of optic canal diameter with optical coherence tomography and visual evoked potentials, to test whether optic atrophy tracks canal narrowing (compressive mechanism) or occurs with patent canals (primary neurodegeneration).

selected_evidence.snippet: Skeletal anomalies include osteosclerosis of the craniofacial bones and skull, optic canal narrowing, kyphosis, platyspondyly and abnormalities of the long bones, e.g. undermodeling, widened metaphyses, and constricted and sclerotic diaphysis

assertion.prompt: Is the cerebellar atrophy of BANDDOS a progressive degenerative process, a developmental posterior fossa abnormality, or both?
assertion.rationale: Cerebellar atrophy was reported in seven of eight patients in whom the cerebellum was assessed, making it one of the most consistent structural findings, yet no publication attributes it to a mechanism. It could be developmental (the posterior fossa is malformed in the Dandy-Walker arm of the spectrum), degenerative (calcifications occur in cerebellar white matter), or both, and serial imaging distinguishing hypoplasia from progressive volume loss has not been reported. This entry deliberately draws no causal edge to this phenotype rather than guessing between the developmental and degenerative arms.

proposed_experiments.name: Serial cerebellar volumetry across the BANDDOS disease course
proposed_experiments.description: Quantify cerebellar volume longitudinally in BANDDOS patients from the earliest available scan, distinguishing static hypoplasia (developmental) from progressive volume loss (degenerative), and correlate with the presence of posterior fossa malformation and cerebellar calcification.

selected_evidence.snippet: Calcifications can also be found in the cerebellar white matter

assertion.prompt: What produces the craniofacial dysmorphism of BANDDOS - craniofacial osteosclerosis, a developmental role of CSF1R-dependent macrophages in craniofacial morphogenesis, or both?
assertion.rationale: Dysmorphic features occur in 41% of cases and are absent from adult-onset CSF1R-ALSP. Some reported elements (bony prominences of the parietal skull, coarse facies) are plausibly secondary to craniofacial osteosclerosis, but others (epicanthus, down-slanting palpebral fissures, depressed nasal bridge) are not obviously sclerotic in origin, and the literature records only an association between dysmorphism, skeletal deformity, and severe disease - not a mechanism. This entry therefore leaves the dysmorphism phenotype without a causal edge.

proposed_experiments.name: Systematic craniofacial phenotyping against skeletal severity
proposed_experiments.description: Score individual dysmorphic elements across reported BANDDOS cases and correlate each with radiographic craniofacial osteosclerosis severity, to separate bony-overgrowth features from those requiring a different developmental explanation.

selected_evidence.snippet: Skeletal deformities and dysmorphic features were often associated with complex brain abnormalities and a more ominous clinical course; however, they were also observed in one case with the adult onset of the disease.
